title: Objectwise normalized finite descent on a connected abelian tower
statement:
Let $U$ be a scheme and $I$ a small nonempty directed preordered set, and let $T$ be a connected abelian cover tower over $U$ [def-sfb-connected-abelian-cover-tower]. Write $X_i$ for its levels, $X$ for its connected covering limit, $\Gamma_i$ for its finite abelian groups, and $G$ for their profinite limit. Fix an algebraically closed field $\Omega$ and a geometric point $z:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to X$. Let $F$ be a set sheaf on $U_{\mathrm{proet}}$ that is finite constant on at least one $X_i$. Use the labelled copies, labelled germs, normalized universal sections and finite-constancy predicate of [def-sfb-finite-labelled-normalized-section].

There are a finite set $A$, a continuous left $G$-action on $A$, a bijection $e:A\simeq F_{z}$ with the geometric stalk at the image of $z$, and a universal section $s\in F(X[A])$ normalized by $e$. This section is unique for those labels and that bijection. At every level $i$ where $F$ is finite constant, there are a normalized section $s_i\in F(X_i[A])$ and a homomorphism $\rho_i:\Gamma_i\to\operatorname{End}(A)$ such that $s_i$ pulls back to $s$, the $G$-action is $\rho_i$ composed with $G\to\Gamma_i$, and the labelled germ of $s_i$ at the acted point $g z_i$ and label $q$ is $e(\rho_i(g)q)$. On the whole labelled overlap $X[G\times A]$, the pullback of $s$ along the continuous action on labels equals its pullback along the map which keeps the label and sends the base point to the second projection of the given torsor comparison. This map is constructed by the pullback universal property, not chosen. Empty finite labels are included. The Lean bijection uses $\mathrm{ULift}$ to match the stalk universe. No assertion about morphisms between different sheaves or about finite constancy of arbitrary sheaves on the limit is made.

proof.text: We may compute every restriction along a pro-etale site object on the slice site: the object-inverse-image lemma identifies the specified inverse image with sectionwise restriction, and weakly etale localization identifies its site with the small pro-etale site of the object. Thus iterated restrictions in the argument below are literally restrictions along composites. In particular the two restrictions of $F$ to a double overlap are canonically the same sheaf; their comparison satisfies the cocycle identity by cancellation on a triple overlap.

For any scheme $T$ and finite sets $A,B$, represent $\underline A_T,\underline B_T$ by the labelled copies $T[A],T[B]$. Yoneda identifies a sheaf arrow with a $T$-map $T[A]\to T[B]$. Its restriction to the copy labelled $a$ is precisely a $B$-indexed clopen decomposition of $T$. Consequently such arrows are exactly families, indexed by $A$, of locally constant functions $|T|\to B$. The assertion includes $A=\varnothing$ (one map) and $B=\varnothing$ (a map only when $A=\varnothing$ or $T$ is empty). This calculation is natural under restriction to any object $W\to T$.

If $T$ is nonempty connected, each clopen decomposition in Step 2 has exactly one nonempty part. Hence the constant sheaf functor on finite sets has $\operatorname{Hom}(\underline A_T,\underline B_T)=\operatorname{Map}(A,B)$. Its geometric fibre at any chosen point is the original label set: in the filtered pointed-neighbourhood colimit, each locally constant label is constant on the open neighbourhood containing the point, so its germ is that label; distinct labels cannot become equal on a pointed refinement. The empty label set has empty stalk. The same label description and the natural inverse-image stalk isomorphism identify the fibre of $F|_T$ with $Q_F$ whenever $T\to U$ carries the chosen lifted point. Therefore every constant finite sheaf arrow on nonempty connected $T$ is determined by its fibre map.

source.place: Lemma 4.2.12; Stacks proetale.tex, pointed neighbourhoods preceding lemma-classical-point

proof.text: Choose a level $i$ trivializing $F$, with an arbitrary isomorphism $a:F|_{X_i}\simeq\underline A$. Its stalk gives a bijection $a_z:Q_F\simeq A$. Compose $a$ with the constant map $a_z^{-1}$ to obtain $\phi_{F,i}:F|_{X_i}\simeq\underline{Q_F}$. It induces the identity on the chosen fibre. Step 3 proves uniqueness, since the ratio of two splittings is an automorphism of a constant finite sheaf with identity fibre map. Restricting labelled copies to $X$ gives $\phi_F$; uniqueness on the nonempty connected scheme $X$ proves its independence of $i$ and of the initial isomorphism. At any other trivializing level the normalized splitting pulls back to this same $\phi_F$.

source.place: Lemma 4.2.12 and Lemma 5.1.2; agent normalization of the finite labels

proof.text: On $X_i\times_UX_i\simeq\coprod_{\Gamma_i}X_i$, express the canonical comparison $\delta:\mathrm{pr}_2^*F\to\mathrm{pr}_1^*F$ using $\phi_{F,i}$. On the component labelled $g$, Step 3 makes this isomorphism a unique permutation $\rho_i(g)$ of $Q_F$. On the diagonal $\rho_i(1)=1$. On a triple with vertices $x,gx,hgx$, the cocycle $\delta_{13}=\delta_{12}\delta_{23}$ gives $\rho_i(hg)=\rho_i(g)\rho_i(h)$: the second comparison, based at $gx$, has the same permutation by connectedness. Since $\Gamma_i$ is abelian, this is exactly $\rho_i(gh)=\rho_i(g)\rho_i(h)$, a left action. In particular no unmentioned inversion of the given comparison convention is made.

source.place: Finite descent cocycle, agent expansion of Lemma 5.1.2

proof.text: Define $\rho(g)=\rho_i(g_i)$ for $g=(g_j)_j\in G$. This is a left action by Step 5, continuous because $G\to\Gamma_i$ is continuous and $\Gamma_i,Q_F$ are finite discrete. The normalized comparison over $X\times_UX$ is the pullback of the comparison over $X_i\times_UX_i$: both come from the restrictions of the original $F$, and Step 4 identifies their splittings. Under the assumed compatible comparison $X[G]\simeq X\times_UX$, the inverse image of the $a$-component at level $i$ is the clopen cylinder $g_i=a$. On that entire cylinder the arrow is the constant permutation $\rho_i(a)$, not merely that permutation on constant-label sections. These finitely many clopen cylinders cover $X[G]$; the uniqueness of gluing sheaf maps proves that the arrow on the whole scheme is $(x,g,v)\mapsto(x,g,\rho(g)v)$.

If a second trivializing level gives $\rho_j$, choose a common later level $k$. The normalized splitting there restricts to $\phi_F$, so the two resulting sheaf arrows on $X[G]$ equal the same canonical comparison. Restrict along the section $x\mapsto(x,g)$ for each $g\in G$ and take the fibre at $z$. This gives equality of the two permutations for every $g$. Thus the continuous action is independent of the level. Notice that equality of these actions is deduced from the sheaf-arrow equality already proved in Step 6, not used to infer that equality.
